To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

we have identified a set of natural haplotypes within the 5′ UTR of Arabidopsis LATE ELONGATION HYPOCOTYLS (LHY), examined their global spatial distributions, and obtained evidence to suggest that these LHY 5’UTR haplotypes may affect the temperature-dependent splicing of Lhy transcripts, and thus the temperature-dependent expression of the LHY protein.
we have shown that the spatial distribution of LATE ELongated HYPOCOTYl (LHY) 5′UTRs correlates with temperature, and that LHY haplotypes have distinct temperature‐dependent spicing.

the 5′ untranslated region of the Arabidopsis thaliana clock component LATE‐ELONGATED HYPOCOOTYL contains a set of naturally‐occurring sequence variants that have a global spatial distribution that correlates with temperature and that these variants affect temperature‐dependent alternative splicing of LATER‐ELONGATED HYPCCOOTYL transcripts.
In summary, our research is concerned with
a novel mechanism by which temperature can be sensed and transduced into the plant circadian clock.

the role of RNA folding in the regulation of temperature‐dependent splicesome assembly, which may be important for understanding how plants perceive temperature and respond to it through the control of gene expression.
the evolution of temperature‐sensitive folding in the 5’UTR of LHY and the role of this in the response of plants to temperature.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
LHY 5'UTR splicing may contribute to temperature‐dependent regulation of the plant circadian clock.
LHY haplotype is associated with temperature and may be a component of temperature‐dependent spicing of LHY transcripts in the 5’UTR.

the LHY 1‐intron 5′UTRs of Arabidopsis accessions have evolved to be sensitive to temperature and that the LHY‐1‐intron‐5′UTR haplotype is a potential marker of temperature‐dependent phenotypes in Arabidopsis.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

haplotypes of a 5′UTRs of a central clock‐regulatory component can be associated with global spatial distribution and that these associations may be informative for the evolutionary history and ecology of Arabidopsis thaliana.

temperature‐sensitive splicing of the LATE ELONGATION HYPOCOTYLS (LHY) 5′UTRs is a likely contributor to the ability of plants to respond to changes in temperature, a process that may be tuned to specific temperature regimes.

the spatial distribution of Arabidopsis LHY haplotypes is correlated with global bioclinatic variables and that the 5′‐UTR of LHY transcripts may be involved in the perception of temperature and/or the response to temperature.
The main takeaway from our work is that
5′UTRs may be important for the regulation of gene expression by temperature and that the 5′ UTR of LHY is a likely target for temperature‐sensitive regulation.

the LHY 1st intron may play a role in temperature perception and response, and that the LHY haplotype may be informative of temperature‐dependent splicings of the first introns in the 5'UTRs of other genes.
natural variation of the 5′ UTR splicing of Lhy may be an important factor in plant temperature perception and response.
